_areas_note: All five peaks sit on one continuous olivine crest running roughly northwest to southeast, and the linking scramble is the reason to camp here at all. From north to south the order is North Twin Sister, South Twin Sister, then Jaw's Tooth, then Skookum Peak (also called Kloke), then Little Sister, then Cinderella Peak, with lower summits continuing south beyond the scope of these routes. None of the five is misassigned. Two trailheads serve the zone and they approach opposite ends of the same ridge. The northwest approach is the Middle Fork Nooksack river bridge and the quarry and Dailey Prairie logging road system, which is how North Twin and the west ridge of South Twin are normally reached; the roads and lower forest there are private industrial timberland with a locked gate, and the standard practice is to bike the road and stash the bike at the prairie. The southeast approach is the Elbow Lake trail out of the Middle Fork valley, with a blazed climbers path branching off toward the Green Creek cirque; that is the practical way in for Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella, and it is how the Green Creek circuit links South Twin to Cinderella in one push. So Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella belong to this zone but usually to the Green Creek side of it rather than to Dailey Prairie. The high crest, including all five summits, is national forest inside a wilderness unit, where dispersed camping is legal. Everything below and west of it that you must cross to get there is private timberland where camping and fires are not permitted, and access there now runs through a landowner permit that did not exist a few years ago. There is essentially no designated camping anywhere in this zone.

sites.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
sites.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted
sites.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
sites.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than trusting older beta.
sites.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.

sites.name: Orsino Creek Basin
sites.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents
sites.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
sites.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
sites.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.

sites.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
sites.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy
sites.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
sites.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
sites.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.

sites.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
sites.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags
sites.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
sites.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
sites.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.

sites.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
sites.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out
sites.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
sites.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
sites.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.

sites.name: Elbow Lake hiker camps
sites.capacity: Two established hiker sites on the east shore
sites.water: The lake, filtered. Reliable all season, though shallow and warm by late summer
sites.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, within or adjoining the wilderness unit. No overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at the trailhead. Fires may be restricted or banned in late summer. Access is the problem rather than the permit: there is no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at the northern trailhead and has not been for decades, so that side requires a ford that is not safe at high flow, and the southern road approach has been subject to a vehicle closure part way in. Confirm both roads and the crossing before committing.
sites.notes: These are the only established campsites anywhere near this range, reached by a spur off the main trail to the east shore of the lake. They are not on the direct line to any of these five summits, sitting on the divide east of the crest rather than under it, so treat them as a legal and comfortable staging camp on public ground rather than as a climbing basecamp. They are most useful for a party coming in from the south with an awkward road situation, or for anyone who wants a settled night before or after a long day on the ridge. The lake is buggy in early summer and the surrounding ground is boggy in places. Because the road access on both ends of this trail has been unreliable and at least one vehicle closure has been in force recently, check the current status of the forest roads and of the river ford before planning a trip around this camp.
